propositions.statement:
Here dimension means **Hausdorff dimension**. As approved by the user on
2026-10-23, assume explicitly that \(E\) is nonempty. With the convention
\(\dim_H\varnothing=0\), the printed equality would otherwise fail for
the empty set. This is a disclosed addition to the printed exercise.

Let \(n\geq0\) be an integer, let \(E\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty
compact set, and put \(I=[0,1]\). Identify \(\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R\)
with \(\mathbb R^{n+1}\) and use its Euclidean metric. Prove

\[
\dim_H(E\times[0,1])=\dim_H E+1.
\]

The zero-dimensional ambient space \(\mathbb R^0\) is included. A later
formalization using a different product norm must justify the metric change.

For every Borel extended metric space X, A⊆X and d≥0: dimH A<d implies H^d(A)=0; d<dimH A implies H^d(A)=∞; H^d(A)≠∞ implies dimH A≤d; and H^d(A)=∞ implies d≤dimH A. Exponents are nonnegative reals embedded in [0,∞] in dimension comparisons.

locals.declaration: Define D=(dimH E).toReal, the real-value map on the extended nonnegative reals; it is total, with value zero at infinity.

argument.text: Work with arbitrary n and E in H001. Apply E004 to this n and this subset E of Rn(n). It gives dimH E<∞, also when n=0. Define D=(dimH E).toReal. An extended nonnegative real below infinity has a unique finite real representative, its toReal, and this representative is nonnegative; thus D≥0 and ofReal D=dimH E. This uses the ordinary order identification of [0,∞) with the finite part of [0,∞], not compactness or a dimension bound for the product.

produces.statement: D≥0 and dimH E=ofReal D.

argument.text: The real number D from F001 witnesses the finite nonnegative representative required by the exported conclusion. Its private name is existentially closed in the conclusion. Since n and E were arbitrary under the original nonempty compact hypotheses, this proves the full quantified statement. Compactness and nonemptiness are retained in that statement although the finiteness theorem does not require them.

argument.text: Use H001 to fix the original n and nonempty compact E. Choose D from N001, with D≥0 and dimH E=ofReal D. The space Rn(n) is a metric space of universe 0 with its specified Borel structure. It is second countable: for positive n, rational-coordinate boxes with rational endpoints form a countable base in the finite Euclidean product topology; for n=0 the one-point topology has a finite base. The max product with ℝ has the product topology, whose countable rectangle base makes its Borel structure equal to the product Borel structure. These facts verify the ambient conditions of the product estimates and the critical-exponent theorem.

argument.text: Fix an arbitrary real q and temporarily assume L1: D<q. By F001, q>0 and dimH E=ofReal D<ofReal q. Both q and q+1 are nonnegative real exponents, with q+1>0.

produces.statement: q>0, q+1>0 and dimH E<ofReal q.

argument.text: Apply the first implication of E003 in Rn(n), with set E and exponent q. The strict dimension inequality in F002 gives H^q(E)=0.

Apply E010 with ambient Rn(n), subset E and exponent q. The ambient premises are F001, positivity is F002 and the zero-measure premise is F003. Its conclusion is H^(q+1)(E×I)=0 in the max product metric, which is H^(q+1)(Fmax)=0 by the definition of Fmax.

Since zero is not infinity, F004 implies H^(q+1)(Fmax)≠∞. Apply the third implication of E003 in the max product Rn(n)×ℝ to Fmax at exponent q+1. This gives dimH Fmax≤ofReal(q+1). Discharge L1 and universally close the arbitrary q: for every real q>D, dimH Fmax≤ofReal(q+1).

produces.statement: For every real qbound, if D<qbound then dimH Fmax≤ofReal(qbound+1).

binders.type: real number bound universally in this fact

argument.text: Taking the exponent D+1 in F005 gives dimH Fmax≤ofReal(D+2)<∞. Define qstar=(D+(dimH Fmax).toReal-1)/2. Temporarily assume L2: ofReal(D+1)<dimH Fmax. By the preceding finiteness and D≥0, the real representative (dimH Fmax).toReal is greater than D+1. Finite algebra then gives D<qstar and qstar+1<(dimH Fmax).toReal. Thus ofReal(qstar+1)<dimH Fmax, whereas F005 at qstar gives the reverse weak inequality. This contradiction discharges L2 and proves dimH Fmax≤ofReal(D+1). For D≥0, ofReal(D+1)=ofReal D+1=dimH E+1 by F001 and nonnegative-real addition. This is the exported conclusion for the arbitrary original n,E, with no surviving local assumption or dependence on the choice of representative. The same calculation includes D=0 and n=0.

argument.text: Define sstar=(D+max(0,(dimH Fmax).toReal-1))/2. Temporarily assume L3: dimH Fmax<ofReal(D+1). Then dimH Fmax is finite, its real representative is nonnegative and strictly less than D+1, and max(0,(dimH Fmax).toReal-1)<D because D>0. The midpoint definition implies 0<sstar<D and (dimH Fmax).toReal<sstar+1. Consequently dimH Fmax<ofReal(sstar+1), contradicting F005 at sstar. Discharging L3 proves ofReal(D+1)≤dimH Fmax. By F001, ofReal(D+1)=dimH E+1. Discharge L1 to prove precisely the conditional lower bound in the exported conclusion, and universally close the original n,E. argument.text: Fix arbitrary n,E as in H001. Temporarily assume L1: dimH E=0, the antecedent of the exported conclusion. Nonemptiness in H001 supplies a point xzero∈E. This choice is valid even for n=0.

argument.text: Define f:ℝ→Rn(n)×ℝ by f(t)=(xzero,t), and put C=f''I. For any real t,u, the max product distance between f(t) and f(u) is max(dist(xzero,xzero),|t-u|)=|t-u|. Thus f preserves all distances and is an isometry between these metric spaces, hence also for their extended distances. Moreover C⊆Fmax: each point of C has first coordinate xzero∈E by F001 and second coordinate in I.

produces.statement: f is an isometry ℝ→Rn(n)×ℝ for the max metric, and C=f''I⊆Fmax.

argument.text: Apply M007 to the isometry f and set I. It gives dimH C=dimH I. Apply E005 to the usual closed real interval I=[0,1], obtaining dimH I=1; hence dimH C=1.

argument.text: Apply M006 to C⊆Fmax in the max product, using F002. It gives dimH C≤dimH Fmax; F003 therefore yields 1≤dimH Fmax. Under L1, dimH E+1=0+1=1, so this is exactly dimH E+1≤dimH Fmax. Discharge L1 and universally close the original n,E to obtain the exported conclusion. The conclusion is independent of the chosen point xzero.

locals.declaration: Fix an arbitrary subset C of Rn(n); no nonemptiness, compactness or measurability is assumed.
Define p by moving the first coordinate to the last: p(t,x_0,...,x_(n-1))=(x_0,...,x_(n-1),t). For n=0 this is the identity on the one real coordinate.

argument.text: Fix arbitrary n and an arbitrary subset C⊆Rn(n). Define e=YuiJoinEquiv(n) by D004. It is real linear by coordinate addition and scalar multiplication, is bijective, and has inverse given by deleting the first coordinate to recover the Euclidean n-vector and taking that first coordinate as the real component. For every x∈Rn(n) and t∈ℝ, its Euclidean norm is sqrt(‖x‖²+|t|²). The nonnegative maximum of ‖x‖ and |t| is at most this norm, and the norm is at most sqrt(2) times that maximum, by comparing their squares. Thus e is bounded by sqrt(2) times the max product norm, and its inverse is bounded by the Euclidean norm. Applying these bounds to differences proves continuity of e and its inverse. Hence e is a continuous real linear equivalence between the max-norm product Rn(n)×ℝ and Rn(n+1). This also verifies directly the property of the composition specified in D004. At n=0 the empty coordinate sum is zero, and these formulas and inverse remain valid.

produces.statement: e=YuiJoinEquiv(n) is a continuous real linear equivalence from the max-norm real normed space Rn(n)×ℝ onto Rn(n+1), including n=0.

argument.text: Apply E008 with real normed spaces Rn(n)×ℝ and Rn(n+1), equivalence e from F001, and arbitrary subset C×I. It yields dimH(e''(C×I))=dimH(C×I), where the right hand product has the max metric and the left hand ambient space has its Euclidean metric. No regularity property of C is needed.

produces.statement: dimH(e''(C×I))=dimH(C×I), using Euclidean metric on the image and max metric on the product.

argument.text: Define p on Rn(n+1) by p(t,x_0,...,x_(n-1))=(x_0,...,x_(n-1),t). For any two vectors, the sum of the squares of their coordinate differences is unchanged by this finite permutation. Taking nonnegative square roots shows equality of Euclidean distances, so p is an isometry. In particular p''(e''(C×I)) is precisely the coordinate realization of C×I with the interval coordinate last. At n=0 p is the identity and this conclusion still holds.

produces.statement: p is an isometry of Rn(n+1), and p''(e''(C×I)) is the interval-last Euclidean realization of C×I; this includes n=0.

argument.text: Apply M007 to p and the Euclidean set e''(C×I), using F003. It gives dimH(p''(e''(C×I)))=dimH(e''(C×I)). Together with F002, this proves the metric-transfer equality for either coordinate order. The subset C was arbitrary, so universally closing C proves the equality for every E⊆Rn(n), without a nonempty or compact restriction. In particular H001 identifies the original current Fmax=E×I and its Euclidean image Feuc=e''Fmax, giving dimH Feuc=dimH Fmax, with the interval-last image carried by p. Universally closing n proves all clauses of the exported conclusion, including n=0. No equality of the two Hausdorff measures is asserted or used.

C×I is an arbitrary subset of V; no measurability, compactness or nonemptiness is assumed.

argument.text: For arbitrary n and E satisfying H001, instantiate N005 at this nonempty compact E. It gives dimH Fmax=dimH E+1 in the max product metric. Instantiate N006 at the same n,E: the Euclidean image Feuc has dimension dimH Fmax, and the interval-last coordinate realization is isometric to Feuc and has the same dimension. Substituting N005 into this equality gives dimH Feuc=dimH E+1, and hence dimH(E×[0,1])=dimH E+1 in the requested Euclidean (n+1)-space. Definitions D002–D005 identify the exact interval, product, image and coordinate order. Universally closing n,E proves P for every n≥0, including n=0. The original compactness condition is retained, though no estimate in this selected basis route needs it; nonemptiness was used in the zero-dimensional lower bound.
